title: Buddhism: everything changes

lines: THE GOOD WILL STAY, THE BAD WILL LAST.
cards: Scroll back through your photos five years. The haircut. The friends you don't see anymore.
The apartment. The face, a bit younger. Nothing dramatic happened, and yet almost everything is different.
It's easy to know this and still treat the good things as if they'll stay exactly as they are, and the bad things as if they'll last forever.
The Buddha named this as one of the main reasons life never quite satisfies, and, surprisingly, one of the main ways through. Its Pali name: anicca.

teach.b: Anicca is a Pali word. Nicca means lasting, constant; the a in front means not. So anicca: not lasting, impermanent.
Buddhists count it among the three marks of everything that exists, alongside dukkha, and a third, not-self, which is a lesson for another day.
The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse, gives it in verse two hundred seventy-seven.

In Max Müller's 1881 translation it begins: "All created things perish." Everything that's put together, that arises from causes, will come apart. Mountains, bodies, moods, friendships, empires, this breath.

The verse goes on: whoever sees this clearly grows weary of suffering, and that is the path to purity. Here's the turn. Impermanence sounds like bad news, and part of it is: it's why pleasant things never fully satisfy.
But look at it the other way.
The terrible week will also pass. Anger, even as it flares, is already changing. The habit you hate is not carved in stone.
If everything were permanent, nothing could heal and no one could grow. Impermanence is also what makes the way through possible.

Buddhist texts record that as the Buddha lay dying, his last words to his followers returned to this: all things that are put together fall apart, so keep going, with care. Not a sad line. A practical one.
So the carry is two small words you can say to anything, good or bad: this too. This too will change.

how: Buddhists reflect on anicca in meditation, watching sensations, thoughts and breath arise and pass, and many chant verses on impermanence, especially at funerals and memorials.

o: a calm state where nothing troubles you anymore
a detachment that keeps you from caring about anything
impermanence: everything put together changes and passes

s: it's also why the bad week passes and why people can heal and grow.
the Buddha's last words returned to impermanence
all things put together fall apart, so keep going, with care.
it means everything put together changes: mountains, moods, this breath.

games.q: you're having a wonderful evening with friends. the thought comes: this won't last. what does anicca suggest?
o: enjoy it fully, because it will pass.
try hard to make it last forever.
games.why: seeing that everything passes is meant to loosen the grip, not spoil the moment. this too, good and bad.

practice: Watch your breath and notice that no two breaths are the same: one longer, one catching, one soft. Then widen out to sounds coming and going, an itch that arrives and fades, a thought that flares and dissolves.
Each time you notice something pass, say inside: this too.

wordCard.voice: Anicca. Pali for impermanence: everything put together changes and passes, the good and the bad. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: impermanent, not lasting. Sanskrit anitya.

carryVoice: Your line: this too. Said to something good, it helps you enjoy it fully; said to something hard, it helps you bear it. That's day two hundred forty-one.
